summary: Moonbase Commander is a browser game where students aged 10 to 14 run a Moon outpost for 30 days. Players pick a landing site, then spend limited crew shifts on solar panels, a fission power unit, regolith radiation shielding, a greenhouse, oxygen and crew rest. Every choice costs something else: shielding uses shifts and power, potatoes give more food than greens but need more power, and lunar night forces a choice between batteries and nuclear power. Real solar flares from NASA’s DONKI database arrive as in-game events, and players decide whether to shelter or keep working. When a mission fails, a report explains what went wrong and what real engineers do about it. The game turns mission trade-offs into decisions students feel directly.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Moonbase Commander is a browser game where a student runs a Moon outpost with four astronauts for 30 days. The player picks a landing site (Peak of eternal light, Crater rim near ice, or Sunny plains) and a difficulty (Cadet or Commander). Each day the crew has a few work shifts to spend on solar panels, a fission power unit, regolith radiation shielding, a greenhouse, oxygen servicing, rest and moonwalks. The top bar shows battery, oxygen, food, radiation dose and morale. A strip shows sunny and dark days, so the player must plan for the lunar night.

HOW IT TEACHES TRADE-OFFS

Every choice costs something else. Shielding uses shifts and power. Solar panels make nothing at night, while a fission unit works day and night but takes three shifts to build and adds a little radiation. Potatoes give more food than salad greens but need more power. Power saver mode saves electricity but slows the garden and lowers morale. Moonwalks lift morale but expose the crew to radiation. Before the player confirms a build, the game shows its cost and effect, and a Mission Control panel warns about coming dark days and the projected radiation dose.

NASA DATA

The game fetches real solar flares from the last 30 days from NASA's DONKI space weather database (NASA Open APIs) and turns them into in-game events. The player decides whether to shelter the crew or keep working. If the browser cannot reach NASA, the game uses sample flares and clearly labels them "sample event". Science facts in the Mission Report come from NASA public information, and the daily radiation level is based on the Chang'e-4 lunar surface measurement.

MISSION REPORT

When the mission ends, or when the player opens the report, the game shows what happened, a chart of resources over time, and what real engineers do about the problem that ended the mission, plus real space science facts. Failing teaches as much as winning.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Students aged about 10 to 14 feel why a real mission needs shielding, backup power and a garden, without reading an engineering textbook. Sessions are short, the language is simple, and Cadet mode is forgiving. The goal is to make mission trade-offs tangible and fun, and to spark interest in space engineering.

TOOLS

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no backend and no install. Inline SVG for the animated scene, Web Audio API for sound effects, and the NASA DONKI API for live data. Fonts: Fredoka and Nunito (Google Fonts). Hosted on GitHub Pages.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

The game feels like a game, not a quiz: a full-screen animated base with day and night, a build bar, floating number feedback, solar flare "incoming transmission" events with real data, and a day timeline that makes planning visible.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy versus fun: game numbers are simplified so the game is readable, and all of them live in one config block. Audience: simple language, big buttons, short sessions, and two difficulty levels. Reliability: the game works offline with sample flares. Honesty: real and sample data are labelled, and the game is not endorsed by NASA.

USE OF SI

The code, design, text and demo video were produced with SI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) and tested and reviewed by the team. The demo video carries a visible SI watermark.
